Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
500 PM PDT Tue Oct 27 2026

For the eastern and central North Pacific east of 180 longitude:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Tropical
Storm Vance, located several hundred miles west-southwest of
Manzanillo, Mexico.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected during the next 7 days.

item.title: Tropical Storm Vance Public Advisory Number 27
item.description:
Issued at 800 PM MST Tue Oct 27 2026 
000
WTPZ32 KNHC 280234
TCPEP2
 
BULLETIN
Tropical Storm Vance Advisory Number  27
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP222026
800 PM MST Tue Oct 27 2026
 
...VANCE CONTINUES TO MOVE SLOWLY TO THE NORTHWEST...
 
 
SUMMARY OF 800 PM MST...0300 UTC...INFORMATION
----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...17.3N 108.4W
ABOUT 295 MI...470 KM WSW OF MANZANILLO MEXICO
ABOUT 275 MI...445 KM SW OF CABO CORRIENTES MEXICO
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...40 MPH...65 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...NW OR 315 DEGREES AT 8 MPH...13 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...1003 MB...29.62 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
Interests along the southwestern and west-central coasts of Mexico
and the southern Baja California Peninsula should monitor the
progress of Vance.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 800 PM MST (0300 UTC), the center of Tropical Storm Vance was
located near latitude 17.3 North, longitude 108.4 West. Vance is
moving toward the northwest near 8 mph (13 km/h). A gradual turn
toward the north is expected through midweek.
 
Maximum sustained winds are near 40 mph (65 km/h) with higher gusts.
Little change in strength is forecast during the next couple of
days, and Vance could become a post-tropical cyclone during this
time if it is unable to sustain organized convection.
 
Tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 70 miles (110 km)
from the center.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 1003 mb (29.62 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
RAINFALL: Through Thursday, Vance is expected to produce 2 to 4 
inches of rain across central and southern Sinaloa, western Durango, 
and northwestern Nayarit, with isolated higher totals of 7 inches 
possible over central and southern Sinaloa.  This rainfall may 
produce flooding and mudslides, especially in areas along steep 
terrain.
 
For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with Vance,
please see the National Weather Service Storm Total Rainfall Graphic
available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_ep2.shtml?rainqpf.
 
SURF: Swells generated by Vance will affect coastal portions of
southern, southwestern, and west-central Mexico during the next few
days. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip
current conditions. Please consult products from your local weather
office.
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 200 AM MST.
 
$$
Forecaster Katz/Beven

item.title: Tropical Storm Vance Forecast Discussion Number 27
item.description:
Issued at 800 PM MST Tue Oct 27 2026 
000
WTPZ42 KNHC 280235
TCDEP2
 
Tropical Storm Vance Discussion Number  27
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       EP222026
800 PM MST Tue Oct 27 2026

The structure of Vance continues to be heavily sheared and ragged 
based on the current visible satellite imagery. Some of the most 
recent images have shown that a small convective burst has occurred 
near the center, however it is also being blown away by the westerly 
wind shear at this point. In addition to the shear, there is dry air 
that is getting into the core of the storm, which is keeping the 
center of Vance fully exposed. The most recent objective intensity 
estimates from UW-CIMSS are in the range of 28-33 kt, while the 
latest TAFB Dvorak fix is a T2.0/30 kt. Given the available data the 
initial intensity has been held at 35 kt for this advisory. 

Vance is moving northwestward at 310/07 kt, as the storm is being 
steered by a low-level ridge centered over the south-central United 
States. A gradual turn toward the north is forecast over the next 
few days due to a strong mid-level trough moving across the U.S. 
West Coast. As a result, Vance should move toward the Gulf of 
California by Thursday. The current NHC track forecast is very 
similar to the previous one, with some minor adjustments being made 
based on the latest HCCA and GDMI forecast aids. 
 
The intensity portion of the forecast has plenty of uncertainties 
due to a variety of variables. The cyclone is over warm waters of 
29-30 C for the next several days, but the wind shear is expected to 
be around 40 kt based on the GFS and ECMWF SHIPS guidance. This 
could allow for convection to develop near the center, but that 
convection will then be blown away by the shear. This could also 
mean that there could be brief fluctuations in intensity at times 
due to the convection. The most recent GFS and ECMWF simulated 
satellite guidance shows that there could be one or two more 
convective bursts from Vance due to some upper-level divergence 
sometime tomorrow. However, the impacts that this convection could 
have on the storm are still uncertain. At this point, the cyclone is 
still expected to become post-tropical around 36 h. By 60 h, it is 
expected to be a post-tropical remnant low, and finally by 72 h the 
circulation of Vance is forecast to dissipate. If the storm cannot 
maintain organized deep convection, it is possible that Vance could 
transition to a post-tropical cyclone sooner than currently 
forecast.  
 
 
Key Messages:
 
1. Periods of heavy rainfall associated with Vance will impact 
portions of western Mexico during much of this week. This rainfall 
may produce flooding and mudslides across central and southern 
Sinaloa, western Durango, and northwestern Nayarit, especially in 
areas along steep terrain.
 
2. Interests along the southwestern and west-central coasts of
Mexico and the southern Baja California Peninsula should monitor the
progress of Vance.
 
 
FORECAST POSITIONS AND MAX WINDS

 24H  29/0000Z 20.2N 108.5W   35 KT  40 MPH

$$
